name: chlorophyll a
provenance: chlorophyll a, the magnesium porphyrin that makes a leaf green. Molar mass from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights over the accepted C55H72MgN4O5 formula; density 1.079 g/mL is a standard reference value and the molar heat capacity is a Kopp's-rule estimate and an explicit teaching approximation. No InChIKey is asserted: this record stands for the chlorophyll of a leaf, and chlorophyll b and the several allomers a real extract contains are not distinguished. The colour is RECORDED, not computed: chlorophyll looks green because it absorbs strongly in the blue near 430 nm and in the red near 665 nm and reflects what is left, and this species carries no absorption spectrum, so nothing in a run derives the green from those two bands. Photosynthesis is not modelled anywhere on this bench, so holding the pigment is not holding the process.

name: nylon 6,6 (repeat unit)
provenance: nylon 6,6 as one adipamide repeat unit, the same polymer-as-population convention polyethylene and PET already use. name: uranium
provenance: M from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights; Cp(s) and density are the standard reference room-temperature values for alpha-uranium. This entry exists so the bench can answer whether a block of uranium warms itself through its own decay (curiosity corpus th-122), and it is a metal on a ledger rather than a metal on a shelf: no acquisition, handling, storage or disposal claim is made or implied by its presence here. The block is modelled as pure U-238; natural uranium's specific activity is about twice this, because U-234 at roughly 54 ppm sits in secular equilibrium with U-238 and contributes almost as many decays again, and the 0.72% U-235 adds a little more. heat_capacity_polys.source: NASA Chemical Equilibrium with Applications (CEA) thermodynamic database, thermo.inp, vendored at vendor/nasa-cea/thermo.inp and documented by NASA TP-2002-211556 (McBride, Zehe and Gordon, "NASA Glenn Coefficients for Calculating Thermodynamic Properties of Individual Species"). Copyright (c) United States Government as represented by the Administrator of NASA, licensed under Apache-2.0; the file is already vendored and read by kerotakis-cea, and these records are the same bytes read a second time rather than a second compilation. Each record carries its own literature reference verbatim - Gurvich, Chase (JANAF), Pankratz, Cox - and that line is kept on every interval so the reader lands on the table the coefficients came from, not on this envelope. The NASA-9 form is Cp/R = a1/T^2 + a2/T + a3 + a4*T + a5*T^2 + a6*T^3 + a7*T^4 with T in kelvin, and only a1..a7 are transcribed: the two integration constants b1 and b2 fix absolute enthalpy and entropy, which this tranche does not claim, because a bench that only needs a sensible-heat difference should not carry a formation enthalpy it never checks. What each row DOES claim is a molar heat capacity as a function of temperature over a stated interval; what it does not claim is any value outside that interval, any enthalpy of a phase or crystal transition, and any property of a real impure sample. The 298.15 K value of every curve is pinned against the constant heat capacity the registry already carried for that species, and agrees with it to better than 3 percent throughout - which is the check that these are the same substances and not merely the same names. provenance: carbon monoxide, the product a flame makes when it runs short of air. Molar mass from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights; Cp(g) 29.1 J/(mol.K) at 298 K: standard reference values. name: hair pigment (eumelanin repeat unit)
provenance: A melanin surrogate, and deliberately not melanin. Eumelanin is a heterogeneous cross-linked biopolymer with no molecular formula and no molar mass, so this row stands for ONE 5,6-dihydroxyindole repeat unit, C8H7NO2 - the accepted building block of it - using the same polymer-as-population convention polyethylene, PET and nylon already use on this shelf. Molar mass from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights over that repeat unit. The molar heat capacity, 179.5 J/(mol.K), is a Kopp's-rule estimate over the atomic contributions C 10.89, H 7.56, N 12.66 and O 13.42, and is an explicit teaching approximation. The density, 1.6 g/mL, is the figure commonly quoted for melanin granules and IS PENDING REVIEW: no positively identified source is claimed for it, and it is flagged for reviewer confirmation. No InChIKey is asserted, because a pigment of indefinite length and irregular linkage is not a molecule; eumelanin, pheomelanin and the carboxylated DHICA units a real hair contains are not distinguished, and neither are the red-blond pigments. THE COLOUR IS RECORDED, NOT COMPUTED: this species carries no absorption spectrum, so melanin's characteristic featureless absorbance rising monotonically towards the blue is nowhere in this record, and a run has only a reflective value on a solid. Nothing here models a hair fibre, a cuticle, a melanosome, or the diffusion of anything into one - the pigment is a powder in a beaker. A REVIEWED AQUEOUS SOLUBILITY OF ZERO is entered deliberately, on the precedent the polymers on this shelf set: melanin is insoluble in water, and recording the zero is what lets the bench say so instead of apologising for not knowing. Note what that sentence then does NOT know about: the honesty pass that speaks it asks the curated reaction table whether anything is consuming the solid, and does not yet ask the kinetic network, so while the bleach is running the bench prints a true remark about dissolution beside it in words that read as though the pigment were untouched. That is a gap in that pass, it is recorded here where a reader meets it, and it is not fixed by this record.

name: bleached hair pigment (oxidised)
provenance: The colourless product of oxidising the pigment above, and a BOOKKEEPING SPECIES rather than an identified compound. Peroxide bleaching really cleaves the melanin chromophore into a mixture of smaller, largely carboxylic fragments, and no single one of them is this row. What the row does is conserve the atoms and stop absorbing light, which is the same convention the hypochlorite decolourisations on this shelf already use for indigo carmine, betanin and curcumin: the parent formula plus exactly one oxygen. Molar mass from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights over C8H7NO3; the molar heat capacity, 192.9 J/(mol.K), is the parent's Kopp's-rule estimate plus one oxygen contribution, and the density is carried over from the parent unchanged. Both are explicit teaching approximations and the density is PENDING REVIEW with the parent's. No InChIKey is asserted, because no single molecule is meant. It is colourless because it carries no absorption spectrum and an off-white reflective value - a RECORDED absence, not a computed one. A reviewed aqueous solubility of zero is entered for the same reason as the parent's, and carries the same caveat about the honesty pass.

name: dry ice
provenance: dry ice: solid carbon dioxide, entered as its own key because the shelf has to be able to HOLD it. `add` deposits a species in its standard phase, so a beaker asking for the solid cannot be given the gas the CO2 row already carries, and the two rows are the same substance in two states rather than two substances - the molar mass is CO2's to the digit so that a sublimation conserves mass exactly. NO INCHIKEY IS ASSERTED: the identifier would be carbon dioxide's, and two identities may not claim one canonical key; the phase is not part of the InChIKey and this row is a phase. Molar mass from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights. Cp(s) 47.0 J/(mol.K) and density 1.562 g/mL near the sublimation point are as commonly tabulated, PENDING REVIEW: no positively identified page was opened for either, and published solid-CO2 heat capacities span roughly 37 to 59 J/(mol.K) depending on the temperature they are quoted at. It is read only when dry ice is still in the flask afterwards, or when a `heat` operation warms it

name: activated charcoal
provenance: Activated charcoal, and a SEPARATE row from `C` (carbon (charcoal)) on purpose rather than the same substance under another name. What makes an activated carbon adsorb is its pore structure and its specific surface area - typically several hundred to over a thousand square metres per gram - and NEITHER IS A PROPERTY THIS REGISTRY CARRIES. The two rows differ in what the engine will do with them: the curated Langmuir isotherm in crates/kerotakis-core/src/adsorption.rs names this key and not `C`, and that difference is the entire content of the distinction. Molar mass from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights over one carbon atom; the composition is written as C because that is what the material is made of, and it is not a claim that the solid is a molecule. No InChIKey is asserted for the same reason. The density, 2.1 g/mL, is the SKELETAL density of the carbon itself and is PENDING REVIEW: it is recorded as commonly tabulated, no positively identified source is claimed, and it is emphatically NOT the poured bulk density of a granular carbon, which is several times lower because most of the volume is pore and void - so a volume or buoyancy answer computed from this row describes the carbon skeleton and not a spoonful of powder. The molar heat capacity is graphite's and is a teaching approximation. A reviewed aqueous solubility of zero is entered so the bench can say the carbon does not dissolve instead of apologising for not knowing, and unlike a solid that is being consumed, that sentence stays true for the whole of a run: adsorption holds a dye on the carbon and does not eat the carbon.

name: lactate ion
provenance: lactate ion, the conjugate base of this registry's `lactic_acid` and the key an aqueous tail needs before it can book a deprotonated lactic fermentation anywhere. IDENTITY VERIFIED against PubChem CID 91435 on 2026-09-05 (PUG REST property record): molecular formula C3H5O3-, molecular weight 89.07, IUPAC name 2-hydroxypropanoate, InChIKey JVTAAEKCZFNVCJ-UHFFFAOYSA-M. The parent acid is CID 612, InChIKey JVTAAEKCZFNVCJ-UHFFFAOYSA-N, fetched in the same call: the two keys share their skeleton block and their stereo block and differ only in the final protonation character - N for the neutral acid, M for the -1 anion - exactly as acetic acid's QTBSBXVTEAMEQO-UHFFFAOYSA-N differs from acetate's QTBSBXVTEAMEQO-UHFFFAOYSA-M, which is the pair this row is modelled on. NO STEREOCHEMISTRY IS CLAIMED, and the silence is deliberate rather than an omission: the stereo block here is UHFFFAOYSA, which asserts none, so this row takes in an identifier the position the parent acid's provenance takes in words - fermentation lactic acid is a mixture of the L-(+) and D-(-) forms in proportions that depend on which organism made it, and a yoghurt culture carries organisms that make each. The L-(+) anion would be JVTAAEKCZFNVCJ-REOHCLBHSA-M and is deliberately not this row. Molar mass 89.07 g/mol, which is PubChem's figure for CID 91435 and is also the parent acid's 90.078 less one proton, from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights. Ion Cp is not modelled and carries the registry's shared 0.0 J/(mol.K) for aqueous ions (see module docs); the 1.0 g/mL density is the same shared placeholder every dissolved ion here carries, because solution volume is carried by the liquid phase. WHAT THIS ROW DOES NOT DO IS MAKE LACTIC ACID ACIDIC: none of the three databases this lab loads (wateq4f, minteq.v4, pitzer) defines a lactate species, so until one does, the acid's carboxylic proton is still absent from every computed pH and the unspeciated-acid note still says so. This species exists so that the database work has a key to book into and a conjugate pair to split against, and it claims nothing further.

name: hydroxylapatite
provenance: hydroxylapatite, Ca5(PO4)3OH: the calcium phosphate that minteq.v4.dat spells `Hydroxylapatite` and wateq4f.dat spells `Hydroxyapatite`, and the most stable solid a near-neutral solution of calcium and orthophosphate can make. It is here so that such a solution can be told what it is holding instead of being apologised to: before this row a beaker of milk reported that it was supersaturated against three calcium phosphates that were in the database and not on this shelf, so nothing could come out of it at all. IDENTITY VERIFIED against PubChem CID 14781 on 2026-09-07 (PUG REST property record): title 'Hydroxylapatite (Ca5(OH)(PO4)3)', molecular formula Ca5HO13P3, molecular weight 502.3, InChIKey XYJRXVWERLGGKC-UHFFFAOYSA-D, IUPAC name pentacalcium;hydroxide;triphosphate. The formula is written here in the mineral's spelling rather than PubChem's Hill order because both parse to the same element counts and this is the one a reader recognises; it is also the spelling both database files use, which is what pairs this species with their phases. Molar mass 502.31 g/mol from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights: 5 x 40.078 + 3 x 30.973762 + 13 x 15.999 + 1.008 = 502.306, consistent with PubChem's four-figure 502.3. DENSITY 3.16 g/mL RIDES A PENDING-REVIEW PROVENANCE LANE: it is recorded as commonly tabulated for mineral hydroxylapatite, whose reported room-temperature crystal density runs about 3.14 to 3.21 g/mL depending on carbonate and fluoride substitution, and no positively identified copy of a mineralogical reference was opened for it - the same position the phase-transition and resistivity tranches take, and it is flagged for reviewer confirmation before any stronger claim is made. HEAT CAPACITY 424.5 J/(mol.K) IS AN ESTIMATE AND IS NOT OFFERED AS A MEASUREMENT: it is Kopp's rule over the standard atomic contributions, 5 x 26.0 (Ca) + 3 x 22.6 (P) + 13 x 16.7 (O) + 1 x 9.6 (H) = 424.5, the same explicitly editorial method this registry already uses for sucrose. The arithmetic is written out so a reviewer can check it rather than take it on trust; Kopp's rule is good to a few tens of percent for a solid of this size, nothing on this bench currently heats an apatite far enough for that to matter, and a calorimetric value should replace it if one is ever needed. THE 393.15 K KINETIC FLOOR IS EDITORIAL JUDGEMENT (Kerotakis), in the same position and for the same reason as the 340 K floor on tenorite: it is a stated stand-in for a rate this lab does not model, not a phase-transition temperature and not a measurement. Hydroxylapatite is the thermodynamic sink of aqueous calcium phosphate chemistry, but at bench temperature it does not nucleate from solution - what comes out first is an amorphous or octacalcium-phosphate precursor that converts to apatite over hours to years, and direct apatite precipitation is a hydrothermal preparation carried out above about 120 degC. Milk is the case that forced the number: fresh milk serum really does sit about eight log units supersaturated against this phase and really does not precipitate it, because the casein micelle holds its calcium phosphate as stabilised nanoclusters. So this lab withholds apatite below 393.15 K and says out loud that it is doing so, rather than precipitating a solid a real beaker of milk does not contain. WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED: no enthalpy of dissolution, no melting point (apatite decomposes rather than melting on any bench this lab models), and no single-figure aqueous solubility - the solubility of this phase is a strongly pH-dependent equilibrium, and the aqueous solver computes it from the database's own log K.

name: beta-tricalcium phosphate
provenance: beta-tricalcium phosphate, Ca3(PO4)2, the mineral whitlockite's synthetic analogue and the phase minteq.v4.dat spells `Ca3(PO4)2(beta)`. It is here because it is the second of the three calcium phosphates a beaker of milk used to be told it was supersaturated against and could do nothing about. IDENTITY VERIFIED against PubChem CID 24456 on 2026-09-07 (PUG REST property record): title 'Tricalcium Phosphate', molecular formula Ca3O8P2, molecular weight 310.18, InChIKey QORWJWZARLRLPR-UHFFFAOYSA-H, IUPAC name tricalcium diphosphate. WHAT THAT IDENTIFIER DOES NOT SAY, stated rather than glossed over: an InChIKey describes connectivity, protonation and charge, and not a crystal structure - so this key is shared by the alpha and beta polymorphs of tricalcium phosphate and by the amorphous form, and PubChem's record is the generic substance. The `(beta)` in this row's name is a claim about structure that the identifier cannot carry; what makes it the beta form here is the log K, which comes from minteq.v4.dat's own beta entry (Ca3(PO4)2 = 3 Ca+2 + 2 PO4-3, log_k -28.92, delta_h 54 kJ) and from nothing else. Molar mass 310.18 g/mol is PubChem's figure for CID 24456; the same arithmetic from IUPAC/CIAAW 2021 atomic weights gives 3 x 40.078 + 2 x 30.973762 + 8 x 15.999 = 310.174, and the difference is the last digit of the oxygen weight rather than a disagreement about the substance. DENSITY 3.07 g/mL RIDES A PENDING-REVIEW PROVENANCE LANE: it is the commonly tabulated room-temperature crystal density of the beta polymorph, no positively identified copy of a reference was opened for it, and it is flagged for reviewer confirmation - exactly as the phase-transition and resistivity tranches are. The alpha polymorph is the less dense one at about 2.86 g/mL and is deliberately not this row. HEAT CAPACITY 256.8 J/(mol.K) IS AN ESTIMATE: Kopp's rule over the standard atomic contributions, 3 x 26.0 (Ca) + 2 x 22.6 (P) + 8 x 16.7 (O) = 256.8, written out so it can be checked. It is about 13 % above the value commonly tabulated for beta-tricalcium phosphate near room temperature, which is the accuracy Kopp's rule is worth and is why the method is named rather than the number asserted. THE 1073.15 K KINETIC FLOOR IS EDITORIAL JUDGEMENT (Kerotakis) in the same lane as tenorite's 340 K, and it is the least equivocal of this registry's three such floors: beta-tricalcium phosphate is not a precipitate at all. It is made by calcining or sintering a calcium phosphate above roughly 800 degC, it converts to the alpha form above about 1125 degC, and no aqueous solution at bench temperature produces it however supersaturated it is - what such a solution gives is brushite, octacalcium phosphate or an amorphous precursor.
